source.title: DAMON: A Dialogue-Aware MCTS Framework for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
source.authors: Xu Zhang; Xun-Jian Yin; Ding-Hao Jing; Huixuan Zhang; Xinyu Hu; Xiao-Jun Wan

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It reports harmful-response rates for a suffix-based jailbreak baseline on several models and datasets, testing the suffix component of V4. Its main multi-turn attack is a different method and does not test the token-position mechanism or the other listed bypass methods.
record.gate_note: The paper tests DAMON, a multi-turn dialogue decomposition attack, and includes GCG as a suffix-based baseline. GCG results bear on the suffix part of V4. DAMON and its defense-condition results report harmful-response rates but do not measure prefilling, decoding changes, or getting past the opening response tokens; those rows are recorded as findings outside the listed versions. The paper does not measure fine-tuning, per-token KL, or safety localization in parameters.
record.test_reason: This is a multi-turn jailbreak attack paper (DAMON). Its only results are attack success rates (ASR) for its own method and six baseline attacks. GCG appears only as a comparator in a method-comparison table (Table 1), run with Vicuna-7B-transferred universal suffixes. No unattacked direct-query ASR is reported, so the table cannot show how much suffixes move models off refusal. The study does not measure fine-tuning, per-token KL, prefilling or opening-token effects, parameter localization, or deepening defenses. Its link to the claim is a speculative discussion that jailbreaks exploit a pretraining–alignment distribution gap (loosely V6), with no test of it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that query-aware decomposition and strategy-aware refinement via MCTS yield state-of-the-art multi-turn jailbreaks, and that dialogue-aware defenses are needed. They also speculate that jailbreak vulnerability stems from a pretraining–alignment distribution gap, but do not test this.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a black-box, MCTS-guided multi-turn prompt-decomposition attack, not fine-tuning, token-position KL, or a weight-localization procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by victim model, dataset, and defense. The authors report paraphrase as the most effective of the tested defenses; PPL has moderate effect and guardrail has little effect.

fits_no_version.finding: DAMON, a multi-turn decomposition attack, reaches 82–100% harmful-response ASR across five aligned models and three datasets, judged by GPT-4o scoring 5/5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-turn decomposition of harmful requests elicits harmful responses from aligned chat models at high rates.

fits_no_version.finding: DAMON ASR stays high under PPL, paraphrase and guardrail defenses. The guardrail barely changes ASR; paraphrase reduces it most (to about 60–84%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Common input-level defenses do not stop multi-turn decomposition attacks.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2025)
record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the ASR results. Its human evaluation uses a randomly sampled 20 HarmBench instances and three student evaluators. The authors note reliance on manually defined attack objectives and manually designed decomposition strategies. The guardrail evaluation uses Gemini as a surrogate defense.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 ablation results, Figure 3 efficiency metrics, Table 4 human evaluation, and Figure 4 context-condition results are not extracted: they concern DAMON components, efficiency, human-rated success, or dialogue-context effects rather than the listed version-specific interventions. Other attack baselines in Table 1 are also omitted because they are not the suffix method named in V4. No rows were omitted for V4's GCG results or the included DAMON ASR and defense-condition findings.

untested.parts: all. No prefilling or decoding manipulation; GCG only as a transferred-suffix baseline with no unattacked comparison.
all. The pretraining–alignment gap explanation is speculation only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 verdicts are removed. The GCG numbers are reproduced baseline comparators in an attack-benchmark table, with suffixes transferred from Vicuna-7B and no unattacked control. They do not test whether suffixes defeat refusal relative to baseline, and the 0% cell (r08) is not a challenge to V4. Qi et al. 2023 is cited only for the GPT-4o harmfulness judge.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusals.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Tests GCG adversarial suffixes only. Does not test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes, nor whether bypass occurs specifically because the first response tokens are passed.
Whether safety behavior is localized in a small number of weights or ranks.
Whether training data or the training objective produces shallow safety behavior.
Training safety beyond the first tokens and whether such training holds up.
